original_value: Photoacoustic (PA) imaging–a technique combining the ability of optical imaging to probe functional properties of the tissue and deep structural imaging ability of ultrasound–has gained significant popularity in the past two decades for its utility in several biomedical applications. More recently, light-emitting diodes (LED) are being explored as an alternative to bulky and expensive laser systems used in PA imaging for their portability and low-cost. Due to the large beam divergence of LEDs compared to traditional laser beams, it is imperative to quantify the angular dependence of LED-based illumination and optimize its performance for imaging superficial or deep-seated lesions. A custom-built modular 3-D printed hinge system and tissue-mimicking phantoms with various absorption and scattering properties were used in this study to quantify the angular dependence of LED-based illumination. We also experimentally calculated the source divergence of the pulsed-LED arrays to be 58° ± 8°. Our results from point sources (pencil lead phantom) in non-scattering medium obey the cotangential relationship between the angle of irradiation and maximum PA intensity obtained at various imaging depths, as expected. Strong dependence on the angle of illumination at superficial depths (−5°/mm at 10 mm) was observed that becomes weaker at intermediate depths (−2.5°/mm at 20 mm) and negligible at deeper locations (−1.1°/mm at 30 mm). The results from the tissue-mimicking phantom in scattering media indicate that angles between 30–75° could be used for imaging lesions at various depths (12 mm–28 mm) where lower LED illumination angles (closer to being parallel to the imaging plane) are preferable for deep tissue imaging and superficial lesion imaging is possible with higher LED illumination angles (closer to being perpendicular to the imaging plane). Our results can serve as a priori knowledge for the future LED-based PA system designs employed for both preclinical and clinical applications.

result.paraphrase: Photoacoustic (PA) imaging combines optical imaging’s ability to assess tissue function with ultrasound’s deep structural imaging capability, and it has become increasingly popular over the past two decades for a range of biomedical uses. More recently, light-emitting diodes (LEDs) have been investigated as a portable, low-cost alternative to the bulky and expensive laser systems traditionally used in PA imaging. Because LEDs have much greater beam divergence than conventional laser beams, it is essential to measure the angular dependence of LED-based illumination and tune performance for imaging superficial or deep-seated lesions. In this study, a custom modular 3-D printed hinge system and tissue-mimicking phantoms with different absorption and scattering characteristics were used to quantify the angular dependence of LED illumination. We also experimentally determined the pulsed-LED arrays’ source divergence to be 58° ± 8°. Results from point sources (pencil lead phantom) in a non-scattering medium followed the cotangential relationship between irradiation angle and maximum PA intensity at different imaging depths, as expected. A strong angle dependence was seen at superficial depths (−5°/mm at 10 mm), becoming weaker at intermediate depths (−2.5°/mm at 20 mm) and negligible at deeper locations (−1.1°/mm at 30 mm). Findings from the tissue-mimicking phantom in scattering media show that angles of 30–75° may be used to image lesions at depths of 12 mm–28 mm, with lower LED illumination angles (closer to parallel with the imaging plane) preferred for deep tissue imaging and higher angles (closer to perpendicular to the imaging plane) suitable for superficial lesion imaging. These results can provide a priori guidance for future LED-based PA system designs for both preclinical and clinical applications.
